choices.text: The first three months after onset are the golden period for rehabilitation; active therapeutic exercise can lessen physical disability and may help some people return to an independent life.
choices.note: Correct. This is not the three-hour window for a clot-dissolving injection.

scene: Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and speech therapy are all written on the plan.
ask: What is each one for?

choices.text: Physiotherapy uses equipment such as elastic bands to restore muscle, or works on mobility such as crutches if power does not fully return; occupational therapy uses activity and equipment for daily life and a return to work; speech therapy trains communication and language.
choices.note: Correct. All three sit inside the golden rehabilitation period page.

choices.text: Speech therapy restores muscle with elastic bands, and physiotherapy is only for language.
choices.note: No. Elastic bands and mobility, including crutches, are physiotherapy. Language is speech therapy.

choices.text: Occupational therapy is limited to giving a clot-dissolving drug.
choices.note: No. Occupational therapy teaches use of activity and equipment for daily life and work.

choices.text: Crutches are forbidden and elastic bands are not mentioned.
choices.note: No. Elastic resistance bands are named, and crutches are an example if muscle function cannot be fully restored.

scene: A patient is told the kidney problem now needs permanent dialysis.
ask: When has chronic kidney disease become chronic renal failure?

choices.text: It is stage one, before any loss of function.
choices.note: No. It is the fifth and final stage.

choices.text: When the damage needs renal replacement therapy on a permanent basis, which is the fifth and final stage of chronic kidney disease.
choices.note: Correct. Nephrology is the branch of medicine concerned with the kidneys. Chronic renal failure is the end of a gradual, progressive loss of kidney function.

choices.text: Permanent replacement therapy means the patient is still in an early stage.
choices.note: No. Needing permanent renal replacement is what moves the patient into this final stage.

choices.text: Nephrology is defined as the branch concerned with the coronary arteries.
choices.note: No. Nephrology is concerned with the kidneys.

scene: Waste is building up and the acid-base balance is drifting.
ask: What does renal failure mean on this page?

choices.text: Waste removal stays normal and only red-cell production fails.
choices.note: No. The definition is failure to remove metabolic wastes or to perform regulatory functions. Anaemia is a later blood-result finding, not this definition.

choices.text: Protein waste is cleared from the blood more effectively as the kidneys fail.
choices.note: No. Substances normally eliminated in urine accumulate.

choices.text: The kidneys cannot remove the body's metabolic wastes or perform their regulatory functions, so substances normally lost in urine accumulate and disturb endocrine and metabolic function plus fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance.
choices.note: Correct. That accumulation is from impaired renal excretion.

choices.text: Acid-base balance is said to be unaffected.
choices.note: No. Acid-base disturbance is included.

scene: One patient loses a lot of protein in the urine and also has high blood pressure.
ask: How are uraemia and faster progression described?

choices.text: Uraemia affects only the kidney and spares every other system.
choices.note: No. Uraemia adversely affects every system in the body.

choices.text: Heavy protein loss and high blood pressure slow the disease.
choices.note: No. Progression tends to be more rapid when those are present than when they are not.

choices.text: End products of protein metabolism fall in the blood as function declines.
choices.note: No. They accumulate in the blood.

choices.text: Renal failure is a systemic disease and a final common pathway of many kidney and urinary-tract diseases; end products of protein metabolism build up, uraemia harms every system, and the disease moves faster when a lot of protein is excreted or the blood pressure is high.
choices.note: Correct. Those end products are normally excreted in urine.

scene: The student is labelling the cause diagram in the renal chapter.
ask: Which causes are named?

choices.text: Diabetes, kidney inflammation, hypertension, polycystic disease, blocked urine drainage tubes, and medicine.
choices.note: Correct. Those are the labels on the cause page. No stroke or inhaler list is added.

choices.text: Only angina, asthma, and stroke.
choices.note: No. Those are not the cause labels. The labels are diabetes, kidney inflammation, hypertension, polycystic disease, blocked drainage tubes, and medicine.

choices.text: Diabetes and hypertension are left off the diagram.
choices.note: No. Both are named.

choices.text: Blocked urine drainage tubes are listed as a treatment, not a cause.
choices.note: No. They are one of the cause labels.

scene: Creatinine is 12 mg/dL and the BUN is above 25 mg/dL.
ask: How does the blood-result page read those figures?

choices.text: A BUN above 25 mg/dL suggests end-stage disease, and creatinine of 12 mg/dL is only an early-damage line.
choices.note: No. Creatinine of 12 mg/dL suggests end-stage renal disease. BUN above 25 mg/dL indicates renal damage.

choices.text: BUN and creatinine are elevated, usually in proportion; a creatinine of 12 mg/dL suggests end-stage renal disease, and a BUN above 25 mg/dL indicates renal damage.
choices.note: Correct. Do not swap which number suggests end-stage disease.

choices.text: Both results are described as below the reference box.
choices.note: No. They are described as elevated.

choices.text: Creatinine of 12 mg/dL is the printed trigger to start Diamox.
choices.note: No. Diamox is a metabolic-alkalosis option. This creatinine figure suggests end-stage renal disease.

scene: Haemoglobin is under 7 to 8 g/dL and the red cells are short-lived.
ask: Why is the blood count abnormal in this section?

choices.text: Haemoglobin is usually above that range because erythropoietin rises.
choices.note: No. Haemoglobin is decreased, usually to less than 7 to 8 g/dL, and erythropoietin is deficient.

choices.text: Red cells live longer in azotaemia.
choices.note: No. Red-cell life span is decreased because of erythropoietin deficiency and azotaemia.

choices.text: Haemoglobin falls because of anaemia, usually to less than 7 to 8 g/dL, and red-cell life is shorter because of erythropoietin deficiency and azotaemia.
choices.note: Correct. The page lists this under the complete blood count and the red-cell lines.

choices.text: Anaemia is not linked to the blood count on this page.
choices.note: No. The complete blood count line is haemoglobin decreased because of anaemia.

scene: The renal gas shows a very low pH and the student reaches for the six-step cut of 7.35.
ask: What acidosis figures does the renal blood-result page print?

choices.text: The renal page uses pH above 7.45 as its acidosis line.
choices.note: No. Above 7.45 is the six-step alkalosis cut. This page describes a decreased pH and metabolic acidosis under 7.2.

choices.text: Bicarbonate and PCO2 are increased.
choices.note: No. Both bicarbonate and PCO2 are decreased.

choices.text: The cause is too much renal excretion of hydrogen.
choices.note: No. The cause is loss of the renal ability to excrete hydrogen and ammonia or protein-breakdown end products.

choices.text: pH is decreased, and metabolic acidosis with pH less than 7.2 occurs because the kidney can no longer excrete hydrogen and ammonia or the end products of protein breakdown; bicarbonate and PCO2 are decreased.
choices.note: Correct. This less-than-7.2 line is the renal page. It is not the acceptable box of 7.38 to 7.42 and not the six-step acidosis cut of under 7.35.

scene: Potassium is high in end-stage disease and the ECG has not yet changed.
ask: What does this page say about potassium and sodium?

choices.text: Potassium rises from retention, a shift with acidosis, or release from red-cell breakdown; in end-stage disease ECG changes may not appear until potassium is 6.5 mEq or higher, and potassium can fall with potassium-wasting diuretics or during dialysis. Sodium may be low if the kidney wastes sodium, or it may be normal.
choices.note: Correct. A falling potassium on dialysis is printed as possible. It is not an automatic further rise.

choices.text: ECG changes are said to start as soon as potassium is only slightly raised, well below 6.5 mEq.
choices.note: No. In end-stage disease ECG changes may not occur until potassium is 6.5 mEq or higher.

choices.text: Dialysis and potassium-wasting diuretics raise potassium further.
choices.note: No. Potassium may be decreased in those two situations.

choices.text: Sodium is always high because the kidney cannot waste sodium.
choices.note: No. Sodium may be low if the kidney wastes sodium, or it may be normal.

scene: The family asks what treatment remains once the kidneys are at end stage.
ask: How many options does the page allow, and which is used most?

choices.text: Three equal options: a salt-free diet alone, a clot-dissolving drug, and oxygen.
choices.note: No. The page says there are only two treatment options, and the first is dialysis.

choices.text: Only two. Dialysis is the first and most widely used, because the chief problem is buildup of waste, and dialysis filters that waste outside the body.
choices.note: Correct. A kidney transplant is the other option and is discussed as generally better but less practical. It is not the most widely used one.

choices.text: Transplant is the most widely used first option.
choices.note: No. Dialysis is the most widely employed option. Transplant is considered better but less practical.

choices.text: Waste buildup is not a concern at end stage.
choices.note: No. The chief concern is the buildup of waste.

scene: The patient is booked for the common machine treatment.
ask: How is haemodialysis described?

choices.text: Fluid stays in the abdomen overnight and the blood never enters a machine.
choices.note: No. That pattern is closer to peritoneal dialysis. Haemodialysis pulls blood into a machine and returns it.

choices.text: The machine adds waste before the blood returns.
choices.note: No. The machine filters waste out.

choices.text: Blood is pulled into a machine that filters out the waste, and the cleaned blood is pumped back; it is practical but intensive.
choices.note: Correct. It is the most common form of dialysis on this page. It is not fluid left to dwell in the abdomen.

choices.text: It is described as a cure for the underlying kidney disease.
choices.note: No. This page calls it a practical but intensive filter. The cure claim is denied on the peritoneal-dialysis page for that method too.

scene: A relative offers a kidney and asks why transplant is not automatic.
ask: Why is transplant called better yet less practical?

choices.text: The supply of kidneys is higher than demand, so compatibility does not matter.
choices.note: No. Demand is much higher than supply, and immunological compatibility is required.

choices.text: Transplant is considered a worse solution than dialysis.
choices.note: No. It is generally considered a better solution, but it lacks practicality.

choices.text: Any patient can receive a kidney whatever the age or other disease.
choices.note: No. Age and underlying conditions can make a patient ineligible.

choices.text: It is generally a better solution than intensive dialysis, but demand is much higher than supply, the donor and recipient must be immunologically compatible, and age or other conditions can make a patient ineligible.
choices.note: Correct. The donation process also has general eligibility requirements.

scene: Home peritoneal dialysis is planned, and the patient hopes it will heal the kidney disease.
ask: What can peritoneal dialysis do, and what can it not do?

choices.text: It does not cure or treat the underlying kidney disease; it is done at home to replace as many functions of the failing kidneys as possible, mainly by removing extra fluid and waste from the blood.
choices.note: Correct. It is for people whose kidneys are no longer working effectively.

choices.text: It cures the disease, so exchanges can stop after a short course.
choices.note: No. It does not cure or treat the underlying disease.

choices.text: It is done only in an operating theatre and does not remove fluid.
choices.note: No. It is performed at home and primarily removes excess fluid and waste.

choices.text: It replaces heart pumping rather than kidney function.
choices.note: No. It is intended to replace as many functions of the failing kidneys as possible.

scene: The patient asks whether a machine is required for every daytime exchange.
ask: How is continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis set out?

choices.text: Usually one exchange a week, with the person kept in bed on a machine all day.
choices.note: No. It is usually three daytime exchanges, no machine is needed, and the person can walk about.

choices.text: Usually three exchanges during the day plus an overnight dwell; a machine is not needed, the person can walk about while fluid is in the abdomen, dialysate is infused at bedtime, and it is drained on waking.
choices.note: Correct. A cycler is only an occasional night-time addition, not the usual daytime method.

choices.text: Dialysate is drained at bedtime and infused only on waking, with no overnight dwell.
choices.note: No. It is infused at bedtime and drained on waking, which is the overnight dwell.

choices.text: Daytime dwells are forbidden and only night exchanges are used.
choices.note: No. The usual pattern is multiple daytime exchanges, usually three, plus the overnight dwell.

scene: The patient on continuous ambulatory dialysis is told a machine may sometimes be used at night.
ask: When does the page say a cycler is used?

choices.text: A cycler is required for every daytime exchange while the person walks.
choices.note: No. Daytime CAPD does not need a machine. The cycler is an occasional exchange during sleep.

choices.text: The cycler means the morning drain is never done.
choices.note: No. The usual CAPD drain is on waking. The cycler is an extra occasional night exchange.

choices.text: Occasionally a cycler does one or more exchanges while the person is sleeping.
choices.note: Correct. That occasional cycler does not turn the usual daytime method into a machine-dependent walk.

choices.text: Cycler use is described as the cure for polycystic kidney disease.
choices.note: No. Polycystic disease is a cause label. The cycler does not cure it, and peritoneal dialysis does not cure the underlying disease.

scene: The folder shows three peritoneal-dialysis examples side by side.
ask: Which names match the three examples?

choices.text: Example 3 is the Ultra bag and example 1 is hospital haemodialysis.
choices.note: No. The Ultra bag is example 1. Example 3 is automated peritoneal dialysis, not the haemodialysis machine.

choices.text: Stay safe is the name of automated peritoneal dialysis, and APD is absent.
choices.note: No. Stay safe is example 2. Automated peritoneal dialysis is example 3.

choices.text: All three examples are glyceryl trinitrate tablets.
choices.note: No. Glyceryl trinitrate is the angina nitrate. These three examples are peritoneal dialysis systems.

choices.text: Example 1 is the Ultra bag, example 2 is stay safe, and example 3 is automated peritoneal dialysis.
choices.note: Correct. Automated peritoneal dialysis is the APD example. It is not a fourth end-stage option beside dialysis and transplant; it is one peritoneal method.
